opening.headline: When you get an error saying your request is too large and the cost is different than expected, learn to measure the size before sending the request and divide the cost into input, output, and cache.
body: When using the model API, you may encounter an error saying that the request is too large, or discover that one question used much more input tokens than expected. It is common for costs to be small when looking only at the output, but the input side of the bill is large.

In this lesson, we'll look at how tokens are divided, what the context window is filled with, the token counting API that counts input tokens before sending a request, the basics of prompt caching, and what the usage field in a response tells us. At the end, the instructor breaks down the cost by solving a scenario where questions are asked repeatedly in a long document.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can explain the meaning of token calculation API and usage fields
You can decompose the impact of input, output, and cache tokens on cost.
Can explain why tokens are divided differently than letters
Describes what prompt caching reuses and its cost structure, and allows you to infer the causes of cache misses.

screens.title: The request is too big and the cost is unfamiliar.
screens.lead: Read about two challenges service operators face. It is good to keep in mind that this is a problem that can be solved by measurement, not by feeling.

visual.alt: Bar graph comparing estimated and actual costs. The actual bar is divided into input and output.
labels: Couldn’t we have known in advance?

paragraphs: One team deployed a feature that retrieved long documents and answered questions. Before long, I was getting the "request too large" error repeatedly. The same question was using much more input tokens than expected.
The cost was also strange. If you look at the output tokens alone, the amount is small, but the input side accounts for most of the bill. I had no idea where the tokens were leaking.

The questions for this class are: Can I know the size before sending the request? And can the cost be broken down into input, output, and cache? Let's learn the tools to measure without guessing, step by step.

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: When guessing the request size based on the number of characters or pages, what items are likely to be left out? Answer this question again at the end of class.

screens.outro: Let's start by measuring rather than guessing. First, let me recall your experience.

screens.title: Think about it: character count and token count
screens.lead: When you select each question, the instructor's thoughts unfold. You won't have to enter or submit your answer, so think about it in your head first and then press it.

items.prompt: If Korean sentences and English sentences are the same length, will the number of tokens be the same?
items.answer: It cannot be assumed that they are the same. Tokens are the units through which the model processes text and do not match words. The way it is divided varies depending on the language and content, so it is easy to be wrong if you guess the size based on the number of characters.

items.prompt: Have you ever seen inputs and outputs counted separately in a usage screen?
items.answer: Input and output have different unit costs and are calculated separately. You need to get into the habit of reading the numbers in isolation, because just looking at the totals doesn't tell you which side is driving up the cost.

items.prompt: If you input a document once and ask a question 10 times, how many times will the document be processed?
items.answer: Since previous conversations and documents are re-entered on each call, the document is processed ten times. This is because the requests are independent of each other, so the server does not remember previous input. This is why most of the costs are on the input side.

screens.outro: Let's answer the three questions using the concept of a context window.

screens.title: How are tokens divided?
screens.lead: When you select a card, it flips over and a description appears. Select the right arrow to go to the next card. We organize the reasons why the number of characters and the number of tokens are different in five cards. The split shown as an example is an assumption for illustrative purposes only.

cards.front: Tokens are neither letters nor words
cards.back: The model processes text in pieces called tokens, rather than letters or words. A token can be a part of a word, a single word, a space, or a symbol. So even if you count the number of words, you won't know the number of tokens.

The subword approach groups pieces of string that frequently appear together into a single token, and breaks rare words into smaller pieces. Byte pair encoding is a representative method, and its advantage is that even rare words can be expressed as a combination of small pieces. As a hypothetical example, happiness can be divided into two parts: happi and ness.

cards.front: The number of tokens varies depending on the language and content.
cards.back: Which pieces the tokenizer puts together depends on how often the text is seen during training. So, even in sentences with the same meaning, the number of fragments tends to vary depending on the language, and a Korean sentence may have a different number of tokens than an English sentence with the same meaning. Uncommon strings such as numbers, codes, and long unique names are also prone to fragmentation.

Which fragment list is used varies from tokenizer to tokenizer. Even if the text is the same, the number of tokens may vary if the model is different. Therefore, the request size must be counted using the counting function of the model to be used, and the counted value from another model must not be copied directly.

cards.front: The number of tokens is both the limit and the cost.
cards.back: The size of the context window, upper output length limit, and unit cost of input and output are all determined in token units. So, rather than guessing by the number of characters or pages, you need to get into the habit of measuring in tokens. In the following screen, see how the window is filled with tokens.

screens.outro: Now that we know what tokens are, let's take a step-by-step look at how they populate the context window.

ext.title: Sennrich, Haddow, Birch: Neural Machine Translation of Rare Words with Subword Units (2016)

screens.title: How the context window is populated
screens.lead: Let's take a step-by-step look at how the context window fills up as the conversation continues. Select the right arrow to add turns one by one.

visual.alt: A diagram showing step by step how the context window bar fills up as turns accumulate.

steps.title: 1. The window is working memory
steps.body: The context window is the working memory that the model consults when creating its response. The model creates a response token by token, and also includes the token just created as input when selecting the next token. So the response the model produces itself is also included in the window. When using an extended thought, a thought token is also included. Input isn't the only thing taking up the window.

steps.title: 2. Things that occupy the window
steps.body: System prompts, all messages, tool definitions, images and documents all occupy the window. Even though the single line of questions the user enters may seem small, the window is filled with the sum of them all. System prompts and tool definitions that are fixed every time play a surprisingly large role.

steps.title: 3. How turns stack up
steps.body: At each turn, the entire previous conversation and new messages are entered. And the generated output becomes the input for the next turn. So the longer the conversation, the more input there is on each call.

steps.title: 4. Even if the window is large, it must be covered.
steps.body: Even if the window is large, context rot may occur, which reduces accuracy and recall as the number of tokens increases. Studies have also reported a tendency for models to not utilize information evenly within long inputs. The result is that performance is noticeably worse when the relevant information is in the middle of the input than when it is at the beginning or end. Being able to contain something and having to contain it are different. Judgment is needed to select and include the necessary content.

steps.title: 5. Window size varies depending on model
steps.body: The size of the window varies depending on the model, and the limit on the number of images or PDF pages that can be included in one request also varies depending on the model. You need to check the window size and limits in the documentation for the model you are using and then design within them.

screens.outro: Let's continue with how to pre-count the tokens in the window.

ext.title: Liu et al.: Lost in the Middle: How Language Models Use Long Contexts (TACL)

screens.title: Token Counting API Response
screens.lead: Change the input type with the slider. Even for the same question, you can see that the number of tokens changes significantly when tool definitions or images are added. The figures shown are document examples.

visual.alt: Schematic with token counting call and response JSON left and right.
labels: Messages are counted without being sent.
Free, limited to requests per minute

stops.body: The token counting endpoint accepts the same input (system prompts, tools, images, PDFs) as it generates the message. Just put in a short basic message and the response will only tell you the total amount of input tokens, like `{"input_tokens": 14}`. The model is not called, only the size is measured. Calls are free and there is a limit to the number of requests per minute, so you can use it without burden.

Appending a tool definition to the same message significantly increases the number of tokens. In the example in the document, the number that was 14 became 403. This means that the tooltip may be most of the input, rather than just one line from the user. Remember, if you define a lot of tools, you're paying this cost with each call.

Inserting an image increased the input token to 1028 in the example in the article. The number of characters alone doesn't give you an idea of ​​how much an image will take up. Be sure to count and send requests that include images and PDFs.

Server tools, MCP connectors, and image·document blocks in url or file sources produce errors in counting. In this case, send it as base64 and count it, or check the usage based on the usage of the actual response. You should know in advance that this is a configuration in which counting cannot be used.

screens.outro: After the actual call is completed, the usage field in the response is read and confirmed.

screens.title: Basic principles of prompt caching
screens.lead: Switch between the two states and compare cache hits and misses in repeated calls. At the end, you can try to figure out why cache_read comes out as 0.

states.label: When prefixes are the same (hit)
states.body: Prompt caching is a function that inherits the processing results of the first part (prefix) of a request when it is the same as the previous request. The Anthropic documentation explains that the tool definition, system prompt, and message sequence are prefixed, and the content up to the cache point must be identical down to the letter for a hit. If you put a long document at the front and just change the question at the end, the document part will be read from the cache starting from the second call. At this time, the number of tokens read is stamped into cache_read_input_tokens in the response usage, and only new questions after the cache point are counted as input_tokens. Costs are divided into three categories: The first token written to the cache is more expensive than the default input price, and the token read from the cache is much cheaper than the default input price. So the more times you reuse the same prefix, the greater the benefit.

states.label: When the prefix changes (deviates)
states.body: If even part of the prefix is changed, the cache cannot be used from that point forward. For example, if you put the request time at the beginning of the system prompt, the prefix will be different for each call, and reading will not occur even if the document exists. Changing a tool definition also invalidates subsequent system prompts and message caches. Cache has a retention time and expires after the default retention time after the last use. If the prefix is ​​shorter than the minimum length determined by the model, it is processed without error and without caching. In summary, there are three reasons to be suspicious when cache_read_input_tokens continues to be 0. Is the prefix different each time, is the call interval exceeding the storage time, or is the prefix too short? Each company has different methods of specifying cache, unit price, and storage time, so please check in the documentation.

screens.outro: Now that we know how caching works, let's read how each token is identified in the response's usage field.

screens.title: Separate billing for usage field and input/output
screens.lead: Hover over or select an underlined term in the text to see its meaning and cost impact. Check them out one by one.

data.text: The response usage includes input_tokens and output_tokens. When prompt caching is used, inputs are divided into input_tokens, cache_read_input_tokens, and cache_creation_input_tokens, all of which become Included in context window. Since input and output have different pricing and are calculated separately, relying solely on the total makes it difficult to identify the root cause. Usage volume for requests made through server tools is verified under response usage. Additionally, Request size limit is independent of token limits, and if there are many images and PDFs, Request size limit may be reached first.

terms.tip: Number of input tokens that have not been read or written from the cache since the last cache point. For services that repeatedly send long documents, this value accounts for most of the cost.
Number of output tokens generated by the model. The input and unit price are different and are calculated separately. Even if this value is small, if the input is large, the total cost is large.
Number of input tokens read from cache. This is an indicator to check whether repeated documents are being cached.
Number of newly written input tokens to the cache. It appears the first time you insert a document, and you should see it change to a read token on subsequent calls.
input_tokens and both cache tokens occupy the window. Just because it's cached doesn't mean it uses less windows.
This is a limit on the size of the entire request, independent of the number of tokens. Requests with many images and PDFs may reach the token limit before they reach their limit.

screens.outro: I will now explain token composition with the scenario of a long document and repeated questions.

screens.title: Commentary: Token organization for long documents and repetitive questions.
screens.lead: This explains a situation where an instructor asks a question five times on a 50,000 token document. Figures are assumptions for illustrative purposes only. Select the right arrow to increase the number of questions.

visual.alt: Stacked bar graph showing the stacking of input tokens from questions 1 to 5.

steps.title: Decide on a scenario
steps.body: Insert a document worth 50,000 tokens and ask questions about the same document five times. We assume no caching, and that each question has a few hundred tokens of answers. Numbers are illustrative assumptions; actual values ​​should be checked with count_tokens.

steps.title: Question 1: This is the first time the document is entered
steps.body: The input for the first call is 50,000 tokens of the document plus the question. The output is a few hundred tokens. Even at this point, the input is already much larger than the output.

steps.title: After question 2: document is re-entered
steps.body: Without caching, only document 5 will be put back into the input for each call. This is because the requests are independent and the server does not remember the document. So the input is repeated in similar sizes for each question.

steps.title: Conversation records accumulate
steps.body: If you even send your conversation history, previous questions and answers will continue to pile up, making your input larger with each call. The fifth call has the largest input. If the input increases like this and reaches the window or request size limit, you will get the "request too large" error you saw at the beginning.

steps.title: Costs are dominated by inputs
steps.body: The output is small, a few hundred tokens per question, so most of the cost is the input. Therefore, simply reducing the output length does not significantly reduce costs. To reduce this, repeated input must be reduced or cached.

steps.title: Prevention: Count before the first call
steps.body: You can prevent exceeding the limit by checking the input size before the first call with count_tokens. If the document is close to the limit, consider cutting it out or selecting only the necessary parts.

screens.outro: To reduce costs, you need to disassemble it first. I will summarize the disassembly order.

screens.title: Explanation: Breaking down costs into input, output, and cache
screens.lead: The instructor fills in the steps one by one to check when costs are different from expectations. Select the right arrow to move on to the next inspection item.

visual.alt: A three-column breakdown table where each cost breakdown check item is filled in one line.
labels: Is a repeat document a read token?
Fixed part (tool definition, system prompt) size
Compare input_tokens before and after model conversion

steps.title: 1. Read usage item by item
steps.body: Input_tokens, cache tokens, and output_tokens are read separately from the response usage. Don't just look at the total, try dividing it into three parts. Which box is the largest determines the direction of future inspection.

steps.title: 2. Are repeated documents cached?
steps.body: Ensure that repeated documents are treated as cache read tokens. If cache_read_input_tokens continues to be 0, it is a sign that the document is not being cached and is being processed anew each time.

steps.title: 3. Count the size of the fixed part
steps.body: The size of fixed parts that are entered every time, such as tool definitions and system prompts, is counted as count_tokens. User questions may be short, but if the fixed part is large, every call will be that heavy.

steps.title: 4. Reduce old conversations
steps.body: Consider ways to summarize or condense old conversations that you no longer need. If you keep the old turn, the input will increase with each call, and as the number of tokens increases, the context rot, which reduces recall, can also increase.

steps.title: 5. Compare before and after conversion
steps.body: When changing models, input_tokens before and after switching are compared with count_tokens. Token counting is based on the tokenizer of the specified model, so even with the same input, the number of tokens may vary depending on the model, and the amount entered into the context window and the estimated cost will also vary accordingly. Therefore, the same request is counted and compared twice between the current model and the model to be moved, and the counted value from the previous model is not copied over.

screens.outro: Now let's summarize the entire lesson.

screens.title: Measure and disassemble to see the cost.
screens.lead: Let's go back to the first two problems and tie the tools of this lesson together.

paragraphs: My first question was whether I could know the size before sending the request. The Token Counting API tells you the number of tokens for inputs, including system prompts, tools, images, and PDFs, before sending them, and the call itself is free. Requests using server tools or MCP connectors are not counted, so check the usage of the response.

The second question was whether we could share the cost. The usage field reports usage by dividing it into input_tokens, output_tokens, and cache-related tokens. Input and output are billed separately, so for services that ask repeated questions about long documents, input costs dominate.

Ultimately, the context window is a single container that holds system prompts, messages, tool definitions, and output. Measuring what fills the bowl and reducing or caching repeated inputs is a way to control both size and cost.

callout.label: something to remember
callout.text: Don't guess based on the number of characters and pages, but check with count_tokens before sending and with usage after receiving.

glossary.def: The unit in which the model processes text. It is divided into frequently occurring string fragments rather than letters or words, and the method of division varies depending on the tokenizer.
The overall range of inputs and outputs that can be referenced when creating a response.
A feature that counts the number of input tokens before sending a request.
Input, output, and cache token usage fields included in the response.
As the number of tokens increases, accuracy and recall decrease.

This is a function that inherits the processing results of the first part (prefix) of the request when it is the same as the previous request. Tokens written to the cache and tokens read have different unit costs.

misconceptions.myth: If the context window is large, you can put everything there.
misconceptions.fact: Even if the window is large, recall may decrease as the number of tokens increases. What can be contained and what must be contained are different, so the contents must be contained separately.
In a structure where long documents are sent repeatedly, most of the cost is input. Input and output are billed separately, so you need to first disassemble which is larger.
Token counting calls are free. However, there is a limit to the number of requests per minute.

misconceptions.myth: The number of tokens is proportional to the number of characters or words.
misconceptions.fact: Tokens are units of string fragments that appear frequently, so the number of tokens per letter varies depending on the proportion of language, numbers, and codes. The same text may have a different number of tokens depending on the model's tokenizer, so you must count them according to the model you are using.

closing.lead: Summarizes what was covered in this class.
points: The token counting API tells you the number of input tokens before sending the request, and the call itself is free.

The context window contains system prompts, messages, tool definitions, and even output, and is populated with tokens divided by the model's tokenizer. The same text may have a different number of tokens depending on the model.
The usage field is divided into input_tokens, output_tokens, and cache-related tokens and reports usage.

Input and output are charged separately, so if you ask questions repeatedly over a long document, the cost of the input dominates, and the first part of the repetition can be handled by prompt caching.
If you use a server tool or MCP connector, counting is not possible, so check the usage in the response.
closing.reflectionLead: The following questions are for self-thinking purposes only and will not be submitted or graded.
closing.reflection: For one request to my service, where will most of the tokens come from: system prompt, document, or conversation history?

checks.q: When the same Korean sentence was sent to two different models, the number of input tokens was different. What is the best explanation?
options: This is because each model has a different tokenizer and the pieces that divide the text are different.
Since the number of tokens is determined by the number of characters, one side of the calculation is incorrect.
Tokens match words, so they must be the same regardless of the model
This is because the server adds the token from the previous request and displays it.
checks.explain: A token is a unit of pieces determined by the tokenizer, and which pieces are grouped together varies from tokenizer to tokenizer. So the request size should be counted by the model you want to use.

wrong.1: The number of tokens does not match the number of characters.
wrong.2: A token may not match a word and may be a subword fragment.
wrong.3: The difference in number of tokens comes from the way the text is divided.

checks.q: What happens if I try to count the input token of a request with the MCP connector and server tools turned on to a token counting endpoint before sending it?
options: It is counted normally, but you are charged for each call.
The call should be avoided as it exhausts the request limit.
An error occurs because counting is not supported, so check with the usage of the actual response.
checks.explain: Server tools and MCP connectors generate errors in counting, so in this case, check the usage using the response. Counting itself is free.

wrong.0: Tool definitions are included in the token and also significantly increase the documentation examples.
wrong.1: Counting calls are free and there is a limit to the number of requests per minute.

checks.q: I sent the question 10 times with a long document in front of me, but cache_read_input_tokens keeps being 0. Where should you suspect first?
options: Does the system prompt before the document contain a value that changes from request to request (e.g. the current time), so the prefix is different each time?
The cache was not created because there were too few output tokens.
Is the cache disabled because you called the token counting API?
The input tokens were counted as 0 due to the short length of the question.
checks.explain: The cache will only hit if the prefix is the same as the previous request. If the first part is different every time, reading will not occur even if the document exists. It also checks whether the call interval exceeds the storage time and whether the prefix is ​​shorter than the minimum length.

wrong.1: Cache hits are not related to output length.
wrong.2: Counting calls do not generate messages and therefore do not affect the cache.
wrong.3: Question length has nothing to do with prefix matching.
